title: Mark Mitchell transferring to Kentucky: Wildcats land former Missouri big man after court allows fifth season - CBS Sports
description: If Mitchell winds up in the clear for this upcoming season, Mark Pope has a roster with valid Final Four hopes
body:
If Mitchell winds up in the clear for this upcoming season, Mark Pope has a roster with valid Final Four hopes
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    8:24 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        It's a weird state of the sport when the following sentence is true: One of the most important commitments of the college basketball offseason has transpired in late August.On Saturday night, Mark Mitchell, who previously played at Duke and Missouri, committed to play for Kentucky this season. In industry circles, Mitchell had been widely rumored as Lexington-bound in the past week and a half. On Friday morning, he received a temporary restraining order — via a Jefferson Circuit Court ruling in Kentucky — to pursue a fifth season of college basketball. He officially entered his name into the transfer portal (with a do-not-contact tag) hours later. 
        
            
                College basketball transfer portal five-for-five tracker: Grading each move in unparalleled free agency window
                
                    Isaac Trotter                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
And a little more than 24 hours after that, Mitchell made his intentions public. The pick confirmed the whispers that had grown to a rumble in the day leading up to the decision. In picking Kentucky, Mitchell provides a proven producer in the frontcourt at the power forward position and gives Mark Pope one more piece (if Mitchell's legal pursuit keeps him eligible all of this upcoming season) that validates some Final Four dreams for Big Blue Nation in 2026-27.Dramatic offseason perhaps ending on a high noteIt seems so far away now, but there was a point a few weeks removed from Kentucky's season when Pope was feeling severe heat for missing out on a variety of high-profile prospects, including the No. 1 high school player in 2026, Tyran Stokes. 
That's now all in the past, as it could easily be argued that Pope wound up landing two of the four or five most important transfers of 2026. The first was Milan Momcilovic, who picked Kentucky over Louisville in what was one of the more expensive bidding endeavors of the spring. Momcilovic is a stretchy 3-man who hopes to again be one of the best long distance shooters in the country.So long as Mitchell's eligibility case doesn't hit a road block, Momcilovic will have a good contrast with Mitchell in the frontcourt. The 6-9, 230-pound big averaged 18.3 points, 5.2 rebounds and 3.6 assists in the SEC last season and was one of the 10 best players in the conference across the past two seasons. Those two will start alongside center/sophomore Malachi Moreno, who bypassed being a potential top-40 pick in order to improve with a healthy payday in Year 2 under Pope. Kentucky has secured the top-rated portal class of the year, by the way, beating out Louisville.
The in-state rivals, coincidentally enough, are regarded by many coaches across college hoops as the two biggest spenders of this 2026 offseason. Kentucky's other portal commits include former Furman point guard Alex Wilkins, former Washington point guard Zoom Diallo and his teammate who also played at UW last season, Frank Kepnang, a center.No fan base has endured more highs and lows in the past five months than Kentucky's.Kentucky the latest to benefit from the legal routeMitchell is the latest proven college player to double back to school after having a cup of coffee in Summer League — a trend that CBS Sports first reported in more than a month ago. Mitchell played with the Denver Nuggets, but with no certainty of making an NBA roster this fall, he and his representation took to the courts to sue for a fifth year. Former Michigan State forward Jaxon Kohler also took this route, committing to BYU after getting some runs in with the Utah Jazz for about a month.
These two will not be the last, either.The NCAA is enduring a nationwide legal battle at the moment, as the organization voted in late June to allow all Division I athletes moving forward eligibility for five seasons in a five-year span. But players whose eligibility expired this past spring did not apply to that rule change.So now there are more than a hundred former Division I men's basketball players (and others) trying to sue for what they believe is an unjust rule change right at the start of the summer. The NCAA has had two minor but critical wins so far: injunctions in Colorado (which was federal in scope) and Ohio (which was under a different framing) have been stayed, which is to say the courts ruling in favor of the players' eligibility has been paused. Mitchell's case was in Kentucky and seen as favorable. The NCAA will still try to get the case overturned there as well, but predicting which lawsuits in which states will go which way is impossible at this stage. For now, Mitchell is like so many others across the country: hoping that a local judge will give him more leniency than the NCAA in order to keep playing college sports, make significant money in the process — and potentially change the competitive dynamic of college basketball in the process. 
You won't find many Kentucky fans objecting to the process now that they've got what's clearly one of the 15 best rosters heading into November ... so long as Mitchell remains eligible.

title: Zolani Tete dies at 38: Former world champion found dead after shooting in South Africa - CBS Sports
description: Tete held titles at junior bantamweight and bantamweight in his 34-fight pro career
body:
Tete held titles at junior bantamweight and bantamweight in his 34-fight pro career
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:45 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Zolani Tete, a former two-division world champion, is dead at 38 following a shooting outside his home in Mdantsane, South Africa. The South African Department of Sport confirmed Tete's death Friday night.Tete started his professional career 13-0 before receiving his first shot at world championship gold. Tete lost that first championship opportunity when he was stopped by fellow South African Moruti Mthalane in their IBF flyweight title bout.After the loss to Mthalane, Tete went just 3-2 before a 12-fight winning streak launched him into the ranks of boxing's best and most exciting fighters.During that streak, Tete took a decision win over Teiru Kinoshita to capture the IBF junior bantamweight championship. He made one successful defense of that title, a knockout of Paul Butler, before vacating the title rather than face a mandatory challenger.
Tete eventually moved to bantamweight, where he went on to defeat Arthur Villanueva for the interim WBO championship. He would then be elevated to full champion, where he made his first defense of the title against Siboniso Gonya. Tete knocked out Gonya with his first punch of the fight, setting a record for the fastest knockout in a title fight in boxing history.Tete made two more defense of the belt before suffering an upset third-round knockout loss to John Riel Casimero.
Tete bounced back with two wins, but tested positive for performance enhancing drugs in the second of those fights. He was subsequently suspended for four years, a period that ended just weeks before his murder.

title: Giancarlo Stanton injury update: Yankees star strains other calf, may be out for season - CBS Sports
description: Stanton has not played since April 24 due to multiple calf strains
body:
Stanton has not played since April 24 due to multiple calf strains
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:19 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The New York Yankees may be without Giancarlo Stanton for the rest of the season. Stanton, who has not played since April 24 due to two separate right calf strains, suffered a left calf strain running the bases during his rehab work earlier this week, manager Aaron Boone announced Saturday. It is a moderate strain, but it may keep him out for the rest of the year, Boone said. "Unfortunately, he strained his other calf. He was running a couple days ago, had fallen, and the other calf is strained," Boone said. "It's a moderate grade. What that means moving forward, we're not ruling anything out. He'll obviously continue to work to try to get it right and hopefully be available, but obviously we're at a point in the calendar where it gets challenging."   Injuries, primarily lower-body soft tissue injuries, have limited Stanton to 606 of 1,160 regular-season games since 2019. He played 24 games prior to his initial calf injury this season. Last year, Stanton, 36, played 77 games, during which he hit .273/.350/.594 with 24 home runs. When healthy, he's typically performed very well. He's just not healthy very often.   
Truth be told, Stanton may have only had a small role had he rejoined the club this season. The Yankees added Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos at the trade deadline to lengthen the lineup. It's possible Stanton would have been relegated to a platoon role at DH and pinch-hitting duties against lefties in the late innings. That said, if he had hit, he would have played.   For Stanton, this year's ongoing calf issues likely rule out any chance at joining the 500 home run club. He is the active leader with 456 home runs. Next season is the final season on Stanton's then-record 13-year, $325 million contract.
Bellinger set to return, Judge working his way backCody Bellinger will come off the injured list Sunday after missing a month with a hamstring strain. Aaron Judge has not played since May 31 due to a broken rib. He started hitting off a tee this past week and is looking at a mid-September return at the earliest. The Yankees are also without third baseman Ryan McMahon. He has a thumb sprain. A hypothetical Yankees lineup with everyone but Stanton healthy figures to look something like this:  CF Trent Grisham, LHB and Heliot Ramos, RHBDH Ben Rice, LHBRF Aaron Judge, LHBLF Cody Bellinger, LHB (CF when Ramos plays)1B Luis García Jr., LHB2B Jazz Chisholm Jr., LHB and José Caballero, RHBSS George Lombard Jr., RHB3B Ryan McMahon, LHB and Amed Rosario, RHBC Austin Wells, LHB and Ali Sánchez, RHBUntil Judge returns, Spencer Jones will play regularly in the outfield, and it's possible he'll play regularly even after Judge returns. How he and Grisham perform will determine that. Caballero, Jones, and Ramos are everyday players for the time being with Bellinger, Judge, and McMahon on the shelf.
The Yankees have won five straight games and are 73-55 on the season. They're three games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East and sit comfortably in the top wild card spot despite having one of the lowest scoring offenses in baseball since Judge's injury.

title: Deshaun Watson fires back at Browns fans after being booed: 'It's a disrespectful thing' - CBS Sports
description: Watson clearly took the booing to heart
body:
Watson clearly took the booing to heart
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:05 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        While his performance against the Bills did not help his cause in his position battle against Shedeur Sanders, Deshaun Watson likely hurt it even more during his postgame press conference while addressing being booed by Browns fans. Watson, after going 5 of 12 for 36 yards and an interception during Cleveland's 31-7 loss to the Bills, decided to go on the offensive when asked about the boos. "I think the whole world knows it has nothing to do about the performance," Watson said. "It's a little bit more personal than that. So, I think it's a disrespectful thing."To make his point, Watson noted that Saturday wasn't the first time that he felt the ire of Browns fans. He added that he gets treated better by opposing fans. 
 "Last time I played on this field, I tore my Achilles. That same fan base, they cheered when I got hurt," he said. "What does that have to do with anything about performance? When a person gets hurt, especially in your home stadium, and they cheer."Watson said that his experiences with Browns fans are usually only negative on either social media or during home games. He was hoping that the situation regarding the fans' treatment of him would be better given his involvement in the city and after he worked to get himself back in position to compete to be the Browns' starting quarterback. "I thought being away for two years and working myself back from two Achilles injuries and putting the time in and being around the facility, being around the city, doing charity work in the city, supporting the Cleveland Browns, hanging out with fans whenever I do see them, being honest, being the type of person that I know I am and the character would help," he said. "And I guess it hasn't. So that's why I say it's personal. So it is what it is. People have their own opinions. There's only so much you can do to change that. So at the end of the day, I just have to continue to just work on it and strive to be better mentally moving forward."  
Saturday was a continuation of the downward spiral that has been Watson's career, especially since he arrived in Cleveland in 2022. A three-time Pro Bowler with the Texans, injuries and inconsistent play have plagued Watson throughout his time with the Browns. He is 9-10 as the Browns' starting quarterback with just 19 touchdowns, 12 interceptions and a mediocre 61.2% completion percentage. Adding to the frustration that has been Watson's story in Cleveland is the amount of capital the Browns spent to get him. They sent Houston six draft picks that included three consecutive first-round picks in addition to signing Watson to a record-setting, five-year, $230 million fully guaranteed contract. It's undeniably one of -- if not the -- worst transactions in the history of sports.  There's also the fact that the Browns traded for Watson despite the fact that he had already been sued by over two dozen female massage therapists for sexual harassment and sexual assault (in 2022, it was announced that 20 of the 24 women who sued Watson had reached confidential settlements). Watson's time in Cleveland began with him serving an 11-game suspension for violating the league's personal conduct policy. 
In addition to Watson's plight, the fact that he's competing against the immensely popular Sanders doesn't help his cause. Sanders, who made the Pro Bowl as a rookie, went 9 of 11 for 74 yards with a touchdown and an interception against the Bills. Sanders also shined during his postgame press conference when he was asked about the fans' treatment of Watson. "I think we all need to understand that we're all human," he said. "I don't really do things to humans I wouldn't want done to me. ... Just for our fans, I appreciate y'all showing up and everything. However y'all feel about the situation, about Deshaun, think it's more about a bigger purpose than just respect. The respect thing that I feel like should be there. Because we're out trying to do our best and trying to serve the franchise the best way possible. We're going out there every game and doing everything we can do. I don't really appreciate that." As noted above, Watson didn't do himself any favors both during and after Saturday's game. And while it appears that his time in Cleveland is destined to be remembered as an epic disappointment, Watson remains optimistic that there is light at the end of the tunnel in terms of his playing career. 
"I don't regret anything in my life," he said. "I think the Lord puts you in situations for a reason. I don't regret anything at all. I had different thoughts on how it was gonna be, but it is what it is. Sometimes, the tables turn, and I'm patient enough -- because I'm a child of God -- to wait for that change. So, I ain't tripping."

title: Teofimo Lopez vs. Rolly Romero fight predictions, undercard, odds, start time, expert picks - CBS Sports
description: Lopez challenges Romero for the WBA welterweight title in the main event on Saturday night

Lopez challenges Romero for the WBA welterweight title in the main event on Saturday night

                    at
    5:30 pm ET

        Two of boxing's biggest -- and most unpredictable -- personalities will meet in the ring on Saturday when Rolando "Rolly" Romero defends his WBA welterweight championship against Teofimo Lopez Jr.Romero is something of an unexpected world champion, though he's accomplished the feat twice over in his career. Always a popular fighter based on his big personality and strong social media presence, Romero has never displayed elite boxing skills, instead relying on an offense-first style and solid power.In 2022, Romero received his first opportunity to break through to the top of the sport, but he was brutally stopped in the sixth round by Gervonta "Tank" Davis.In his next fight after losing to Davis, Romero won his first world championship, picking up a ninth-round TKO win over Ismael Barroso to capture the vacant WBA junior welterweight championship. That win was heavily tainted by the fact that Romero was getting thoroughly outclassed by Barroso, a late replacement in the fight, when the referee jumped in for a clear early stoppage nearly the second Romero had gathered any momentum.
Romero dropped the title in his next outing, getting stopped by Isaac "Pitbull" Cruz. Two fights later, Romero again found himself playing the "b-side" to a bigger name fighter when he took on Ryan Garcia in New York's Times Square.
        
            
                Teofimo Lopez Jr. looks to bounce back from disastrous loss when he faces Rolly Romero for welterweight title
                
                    Brian Campbell                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Garcia fought the worst fight of his life, turning in a lifeless performance that allowed Romero to win the "regular" WBA welterweight title, and was subsequently elevated to full champion when Jaron Ennis vacated his belt to move up in weight.Now, Romero faces Lopez, a fighter who has always been viewed as a man with elite talent but a lacking mental game, almost the inverse of Romero.
Lopez won the first 16 fights of his career, a run that culminated in a win over Richard Commey to claim the IBF lightweight championship and Vasiliy Lomachenko to add the WBA and WBO titles.Just as it seemed Lopez was poised to take over the sport, he suffered a devastating setback when he dropped a split decision to massive underdog George Kambosos Jr. Lopez was knocked down by Kambosos and clearly lost the fight, making the one card scored his way an oddity that seemed to convince Lopez boxing's elites had conspired against the bigger name fighter with the bigger fanbase and the bigger promoter in favor of a fighter largely unknown in the sport.As Lopez performed a backflip after the Kambosos loss, it confirmed to many that mental issues Lopez had displayed throughout his career -- along with a seemingly unhealthy attachment to his father serving as his trainer -- may hold him back from his true potential.
Lopez rebounded with six wins of varying quality, including struggles against Sandor Martín and Jamaine Ortiz, and a few impressive wins, including over Josh Taylor to capture the WBO junior welterweight title.That run brought Lopez to his most recent fight, where he was badly outclassed by Shakur Stevenson over 12 rounds. Lopez was nearly shut out that night, losing 119-109 on all three official scorecards.Against Stevenson, Teofimo Lopez Sr. offered little constructive advice in the corner, something that Lopez Jr. has taken issue with in the months since the loss, continuing their tumultuous relationship.
"I'm fighting a big puncher at 147 and going up to that weight for the first time," Lopez said at a recent media workout. "We're taking a risk, because it's no risk, no reward. I'm just focusing on my objectives so I can come out victorious."Every fight at 147 will be my biggest fight. I won't say they'll all be the most challenging. The best man will end up on top. Right now I'm only focused on Rolly Romero."Let's take a closer look at the rest of the undercard for Saturday night in Las Vegas with the latest odds from DraftKings before getting to a prediction and expert pick on the main event below.
Romero vs. Lopez fight card, oddsTeofimo Lopez Jr. -300 vs. Rolando Romero (c) +230, WBA welterweight titleYoenli Hernandez -1400 vs. Francisco Daniel Veron +750, middleweightsGary Antonio Russell -180 vs. Victor Santillan +140, junior featherweightsCarlos Utria -1600 vs. Israel Mercado +750, junior welterweightsMarco Romero -5000 vs. Kahlil Mitchell +1300, middleweightsBenjamin Johnson vs. Jose Gabriel Rodriguez, welterweightsJoseph Brown -5000 vs. Alton Wiggins +1300, junior middleweightsAldo Blancas -5000 vs. Ricky Mamone +1300, junior welterweightsWhere to watch Romero vs. Lopez Date: Saturday, Aug. 22 | Start time: 8 p.m. ET (Main card) (Main event ring walks expected around 11 p.m. ET)Location: T-Mobile Arena -- Las VegasTV Channel/Stream: DAZN PPV | Price: $79.99PredictionLopez is the better fighter. He's the man with more natural gifts. He's the fighter with more technical skills. However, Lopez is also a fighter with some obvious flaws. He's shown mental weakness and a tendency to get flustered the second things aren't coming easily in the ring. Lopez has also had extreme trouble with fighters who use movement and don't choose to engage. Sandor Martín took that approach in a fight where he likely deserved the decision, and that left Lopez asking "Do I still got it?" after the final bell.The problem for Romero is that he is very unlikely to be a fighter who is going to take a Martin-esque approach to fighting Lopez. Romero has a strong mental game, and that's a good tool against someone like Lopez, but he doesn't have the style to further fluster and beat Lopez unless he turns in a career-best performance.Romero beat Garcia because Garcia simply didn't show up that night in New York City. Garcia didn't engage and he didn't throw punches, making for an easy night for Romero. Lopez isn't likely to turn in a dud on that level, and all things being equal, it should be a fairly easy win for Lopez. Whether or not Lopez can score his first stoppage win since 2022 is a more intriguing question. Pick: Teofimo Lopez via UD

title: Chiefs' Harrison Butker drills historic 69-yard field goal, but it won't count in the NFL record book - CBS Sports
description: Butker can have bragging rights after his booming kick, but the NFL record stands
body:
Butker can have bragging rights after his booming kick, but the NFL record stands
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:47 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The biggest highlight of the NFL preseason this year just came from a kicker and it happened on Saturday night when Harrison Butker drilled a 69-yard field goal just before halftime in the Chiefs' game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. And yes, you read that correctly: Butker hit from 69 YARDS. The NFL record for longest field goal is 68 yards and Butker actually topped that with his kick, but he won't be getting his name etched into the NFL record book, because preseason kicks don't officially count. Due to that rule, Cam Little's 68-yard field goal from last season still stands as the longest kick in NFL history. Even though it won't go down in the record book, Butker's kick was still wildly impressive and that's mostly because the ball easily cleared the crossbar. Butker absolutely smashed the kick -- the ball hit the net behind the field goal posts -- and his attempt likely would have been good from 75 yards or even further. You know what, let's stop talking about the kick and just watch it. 
Butker only got the field goal attempt because the Chiefs' defense made a fourth-down stop late in the first half. With under 10 seconds left to play in the second quarter, the Buccaneers were facing a fourth-and-5 from Kansas City's 49-yard line and they decided to go for it. The Bucs ended up failing on the fourth down after Jake Browning threw an incomplete pass and that gave Kansas City the ball with just three seconds left. At that point, Andy Reid decided to sent out Butker. 
The 69-yarder was one of three that Butker hit against Tampa Bay to go along with a 58-yarder and 45-yarder, but he also missed a 43-yard kick in the fourth quarter of Kansas City's 16-15 loss. Although Butker won't be getting his name in the NFL record book, he will certainly have some bragging rights and that's because 69-yarder is tied for the second-longest field goal made in an actual game in the history of football. The first American football game was played in 1869 and in the 157 years since then, only three kickers have hit a field goal of at least 69 yards in a game: 
1. Cam Little hit a 70-yarder for the Jaguars during the 2025 preseason. 
T-2. Harrison Butker hit a 69-yarder on Saturday night (The first clip we showed you at the top was from the Chiefs' broadcast team, so now, let's see what the Buccaneers' broadcast team had to say about the kick)
T-2. Abilene Christian kicker Ove Johansson hit a 69-yarder in 1976. And in case you're wonder, yes, there is footage of Johansson's kick. 
College kickers were allowed to use a 1- to 2-inch kicking block until 1989 when they were banned. Before the ban, kickers were essentially kicking off a tee as long as the holder was able to get the ball in the right spot. The five longest field goals in college history, including Johansson's, all came when the kicking block was legal.
With their field goals being kicked off the ground, Little and Butker are in a league of their own. Now that Butker has a 69-yarder under his belt, we might want to keep an eye on him this year, because he could go off like Little did last season for the Jaguars. Although Little's 70-yard kick in the preseason didn't count in the NFL record book, he ended up breaking the record anyway. The Jaguars kicker drilled a 68-yarder last November to break the record for longest field goal in NFL history. The mark had been held by Justin Tucker, who hit a 66-yarder in 2021. Little also hit a 67-yarder in Week 18, and thanks to those two kicks, Little now officially has the two longest field goals in NFL history. The 67-yarder also holds the mark for longest OUTDOOR field goal in NFL history (His 68-yarder came indoors in Las Vegas).  Butker's career long in a regular-season game is 62 yards, so he definitely has a big leg and it won't be surprising if he tops that number this season. Maybe he'll even break Little's record, because at the rate things are going, it seems like it will only be a matter of time before an NFL kicker drills a 70-yarder in a regular-season game. 
Why all the booming kicks?One reason we're seeing more long kicks is thanks to a new K-ball rule that the NFL implemented last season. Under the new rule, each team is given 60 kicking footballs (K-Balls) at the beginning of the season. This allows each team to break the ball in before they use it. Since the ball can be used in practice, that generally softens it up. Teams are also allowed to use a brush to try and rub down the bumps (Every football is covered by thousands of tiny bumps). A football that's broken in tends to fly better and a smoother ball allows the kicker to make better contact, which leads to better kicks. Under the old rule that existed from 1999 until 2024, teams were given three brand new footballs ON GAME DAY and they had roughly one hour to break them in. The new balls were stiff, which made them more difficult to kick. It was the difference between using a brand new baseball glove and a worn in glove. Last season, almost every kicker seemed to agree that the new rule was adding five to 10 yards to their kicks. Bengals special teams coordinator Darrin Simmons has been an NFL assistant since 1998, so he's seen everything, and he thinks the new rule could lead to even longer kicks going forward. 
"I believe it makes a big difference and I think that's why the distances on some of these long field goals went up and I think it will continue to just skyrocket as long as that rule stays in place the way it is," Simmons told CBS Sports and several other outlets in late July. Records are made to be broken and thanks to the NFL's new K-ball rule, it won't be surprising at all if the record for longest field goal goes down for the second straight season.

title: Ketel Marte spotted at casino during Diamondbacks game as off-field drama continues - CBS Sports

        The Ketel Marte saga took another turn Friday as photos surfaced on social media showing the Diamondbacks second baseman at a local casino during the team's home game against the Reds (ARI 9, CIN 0). Marte is currently on the injured list with a knee issue. He was initially placed on the restricted list after failing to show up for a game against the Red Sox in Boston on Monday. "He's free to do whatever he wants," manager Torey Lovullo said following Friday's game (via the Arizona Republic). "That's  how I look at it. As long as he wakes up tomorrow morning and posts, and  gets his work done at Salt River, which I am certain he will, that's  all that matters to me right now." Marte was spotted Friday sitting at a roulette table as a nearby television showed the D-backs game in the top of the sixth inning. After no-showing on Monday, he did not explain his absence to the team until meeting with club officials on Thursday, at which point he was moved from the restricted list to the injured list. Marte left the team in Boston to undergo testing on his knee.   
Players on the injured list are generally not required to attend games. Marte was rehabbing his knee injury early in the day at Salt River Fields, the team's spring training complex in Arizona, which is common practice. Lovullo did, however, say earlier Friday that he felt "betrayed" by the entire ordeal with Marte. 
"I was hurting. I was clearly  hurting," Lovullo said prior to Friday's game (via The Athletic). "Once I saw what was unfolding, I became extremely frustrated,  and I felt betrayed. And that's a whole different type of pain and  frustration. But I'm through that. I'm getting through that." 
        
            
                Ketel Marte placed on restricted list after not showing up for Diamondbacks game over 'personal issue'
                
                    Dayn Perry                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Reliever Kevin Ginkel expressed frustration with Marte, saying (via The Athletic): "For us to go where we want to go, we've got to have him here. It's disappointing how the things  that happened happened. There's really no explanation for it."This is not the first time Marte has frustrated teammates. He was away from the D-backs after his home was broken into during last year's All-Star break, plus there has also been criticism about his penchant for requesting days off. Marte had started 116 of the team's 125 games before going AWOL on Monday. 
Marte, 32, is having a down season by his usual standards. He finished third in the MVP voting in 2024 and was an All-Star the last two years. Marte was in trade rumors all offseason, though Arizona was unable to work out a deal. He gained full no-trade protection as a 10-and-5 player (10 years in MLB, including the last five with the same team) in April. Any discontent with Marte has not stopped the D-backs from signing him to contract extensions. He inked a seven-year extension worth $116.5 million last April. It includes a $11.5 million player option for the 2031 season. That was the third time Arizona extended Marte. They previously signed him to five-year deals in 2018 and 2023. Friday's win improved the D-backs to 68-61. They are one game behind the Padres for the third wild card spot.

title: Class of 2022 athletes just lost their eligibility again but chaos isn't over for college football, basketball - CBS Sports
description: The NCAA's fight with seniors who exhausted their eligibility is just getting started
body:
The NCAA's fight with seniors who exhausted their eligibility is just getting started
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:52 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        In the aftermath of the latest chaos for the Class of 2022 on Friday, a general manager of a college football team sent CBS Sports a message with a meme of Ed Helms' character in "The Hangover."It shows Helms, upon waking up from his group's wild night in Las Vegas, attempting to put his glasses back on while walking around groggy and confused as he began to process the carnage he was seeing around him."Me every day (right now)," the GM joked.He's far from alone in feeling like that among people in his space. In the latest twist in this college eligibility craziness that's been an ongoing saga ever since the initial Colorado district court ruling on July 31 that gave Class of 2022 players another year of eligibility, the NCAA got a win Friday and was granted a stay in that Colorado case. That shifts players from the Class of 2022 players who exhausted their eligibility last season back to being ineligible unless they've filed their own individual lawsuits and been granted their own separate temporary restraining orders against the NCAA.
        
            
                What's stopping Diego Pavia from returning to college football as legal challenges to NCAA mount?
                
                    Brad Crawford                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The chaos is far from over. After talking to sources, he's what you need to know:
Some players remain eligible While the U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals' stay removes the sweeping fifth year of eligibility provided to Class of 2022 athletes in the Colorado case, many other athletes remain eligible because of TROs and injunctions they were granted in court cases on the state level. That includes all the players who gained eligibility earlier this week in Louisiana, a case that allowed players who've signed NFL contracts to return to school. Former FSU QB Thomas Castellanos will attempt to play in 2026. 
                                                                    Getty Images
                                                            Shortly after the Colorado ruling Friday, 10 athletes were granted TROs by a court in Kentucky. Former Florida State quarterback Thomas Castellanos was also granted a TRO on Friday, which now allows him to come back to college for a fifth season and also enter the transfer portal.
Lawyers referred to these TROs as layers of protection against NCAA rules to CBS Sports. The Colorado case granted every 2022 athlete a shield against NCAA rules. Winning a TRO in a state court provides another. So even with the 10th Circuit staying the lawsuit led by Northern Colorado basketball player Brock Wisne, players who gained eligibility in other cases are unaffected by that decision. An example is New Mexico kicker Luke Drzewiecki. He gained his year back in the Louisiana case Thursday and by Friday he'd already signed with Minnesota for his final season of eligibility. Being part of the lawsuit in Louisiana allowed him to both enter the portal -- something those who gained years back in Colorado could not do -- and prevents the NCAA, at least for now, from enforcing its eligibility rules against him. As a result, Drzewiecki could play for the Gophers if the season started today, but players who were granted an extra year solely for Colorado can not.More lawsuits are coming soon One thing is certain in talking with sources in the wake of the 10th Circuit's decision -- it will trigger another significant round of lawsuits in state courts. 
Lawyers and agents CBS Sports spoke with Friday said they expect additional lawsuits filed next week by players who are hoping to gain their fifth years back after losing them with the 10th Circuit's decision. Time is of the essence for football players. The college football season starts next Saturday for some, and everyone will be underway by Labor Day weekend. Expect a rush of lawsuits filed in state courts against the NCAA next week as players attempt to return before the season begins. Even with the football season's start on the horizon, sources across the sport expect the back-and-forth eligibility situation to continue well into the season. It echoes the Charles Bediako situation with Alabama basketball last season. Bediako's status was a day-to-day question after returning to the Crimson Tide following multiple seasons in the G League, and he played only five games with the Tide before being ruled ineligible. 
That was a multi-week saga that enraged many in college basketball. With multiple state cases in flux this fall, you could see players gain and lose eligibility depending on the week and the whims of the courts. A sticky situation in the SEC There's a growing discord in the SEC ahead of the season with this unexpected window of player movement. The SEC maintains strict intraconference rules that prevent athletes from transferring from one intraleague institution to another except for in certain windows of the year. That's something SEC commissioner Greg Sankey reminded schools about earlier this month when he sent a memo stating that the league's transfer rules remain in place amid Class of 2022 eligibility chaos. 
However, when reached by CBS Sports on Friday about whether the league's intraconference transfer rules still applied -- and would hold up -- amid the Louisiana lawsuit language, the SEC declined to comment. The lawyer for the plaintiffs in the Louisiana lawsuit, Ryan Downton, told CBS Sports that "We believe the order should allow players to transfer within the conference, but have reached out to the SEC to discuss."Multiple SEC schools, per sources, believe the league's ban on SEC-to-SEC transfers would not hold up in court. 
We've already seen some behind-the-scenes movement that might suggest that. LSU is eyeing several former SEC players, per sources, who could return to school. On the basketball side, Kentucky is considered the favorite for former Missouri power forward Mark Mitchell, who entered the portal Friday after he was granted a TRO against the NCAA in a court case in Kentucky.

title: College football returning production 2026: What does every roster actually look like this season? - CBS Sports
description: We break down the numbers of which teams have the most firepower coming back this season
body:
We break down the numbers of which teams have the most firepower coming back this season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Aug 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:33 am ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        College football roster building was supposed to get a little easier this offseason. Instead, it somehow got way more complicated than anyone could have predicted.There was no spring transfer portal window this year, only a condensed winter window that still saw a record number of entries. Teams were forced to address major roster needs, departures and additions in a matter of weeks.Then came the five-for-five eligibility rule. Then the federal court injunction in Colorado that opened another path for members of the 2022 recruiting class to return for an additional season. That created another wave of roster movement just weeks before the start of the season, with some programs bringing back players who otherwise would have exhausted their eligibility.And now, apparently, we're still not done.On Wednesday, a Louisiana judge granted a temporary restraining order to 16 football players, including several who had already signed NFL contracts, clearing a potential path for them to return to college football.
For the coaches and front office personnel actually responsible for building these rosters, it's been a summer-long headache. For those of us trying to keep track of all of it, it's been inconvenient.Our process started as teams finished their 2025 seasons, when we began tracking not only returning starters but every player coming and going from all 138 FBS programs (welcome to the club, North Dakota State and Sacramento State) while keeping tabs on how much playing time each roster was gaining or losing using snap count data from TruMedia.We published our initial round of returning production features earlier this offseason using spring rosters as the baseline. But with the eligibility rulings and other roster movement continuing well into August, we went back through all 138 rosters one more time before fall camp to provide the most up-to-date look possible.
All that work produced three different ways of answering the same question: What does each FBS roster actually look like entering the 2026 season?Returning starters are the simplest way to measure continuity, but the transfer portal has made that number less definitive than it once was. Returning snap rates tell us how much of last year's actual workload remains. And career experience shows us how much proven college football a team has on its roster, regardless of whether that experience was developed internally or imported through the transfer portal.Those numbers often overlap, but they also tell very different stories.Here's what stood out.Returning starters: Which teams bring back the most?
        
            
                College football returning production 2026: Returning starters for every FBS team
                
                    Cody Nagel                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
The most obvious takeaway from the returning starters study is that the traditional measure of continuity hasn't become irrelevant. It has just become easier to manipulate.
The teams with the most returning starters naturally have some of the strongest continuity entering the season. Georgia, Notre Dame and Oregon each bring back 14 starters, while USC leads the FBS with 15. Six of the eight teams with the best national championship odds return at least 11 starters.But Indiana is the reason the metric needs some context.The Hoosiers became the first national champion in nine years to win the title without returning at least 11 starters, bringing back only eight players who had made six or more starts the previous season. Miami had the same number. Both programs supplemented those returning cores with experienced transfers and immediately played for the national championship.That is the modern version of roster building. You don't necessarily have to keep your players if you can replace them with players who have already done the job somewhere else.
So returning starters remain a useful baseline for continuity. They just don't tell us about the whole roster.Returning snaps: How much of last year's team actually remains?
        
            
                College football returning snap percentages 2026: Production back from last season for every team
                
                    Cody Nagel                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
This is where the roster picture gets a little more complicated. Returning starters can tell us how many familiar names are back, but they don't capture how much of last year's team is actually returning.Notre Dame leads the FBS by bringing back 66% of its offensive and defensive snaps from 2025. Six of the eight teams with the best national championship odds rank inside the top 25 in returning snaps. Indiana and Miami are the exceptions. The two teams that played for last year's national championship return just 44% and 46% of their snaps, respectively.
Coaching turnover is a common thread near the bottom: 21 of the 32 teams with the lowest overall returning snap rates also made a change at head coach. But there are some notable exceptions. Colorado, San Jose State and West Virginia all rank in the bottom 12 nationally in returning snap rates despite keeping their head coaches, while Florida, Michigan, Stanford and Virginia Tech all rank among the top 30 despite changing coaches.A team can bring back several starters and still have a lot of turnover around them, while another can lose a starter or two but retain a significant portion of the players who made up its rotation.The two measures generally move together. All but five of the 30 teams returning at least 11 starters also rank in the top 30 in returning snaps. But looking at both gives us a better idea of just how much of last year's roster is actually still around.
Experience: Which teams have the most career snaps?
        
            
                College football's most experienced teams: Ranking all 138 FBS rosters ahead of the 2026 season
                
                    Cody Nagel                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Here's where the transfer portal has fundamentally changed how we should evaluate rosters.Oklahoma State returns just 11% of its snaps from last season, 133rd nationally. But it also ranks second in the country in total career FBS snaps. Eric Morris tore down much of the 1-11 roster he inherited and replaced a significant amount of that lost experience through the transfer portal. Virginia took that approach to an even greater extreme, leading the FBS in total career snaps, games played and starts after importing a massive amount of proven college experience.
That's the clearest example of how roster building has changed. Five years ago, an experienced team was usually one that had recruited well and kept its players around long enough to become veterans. Now, a team can lose most of its roster in one offseason and replace that experience almost immediately.Returning starters tell us which familiar faces remain. Returning snaps tell us how much of the team stayed. Experience tells us who is on the team now and how much college football they've already played.

title: Why Paige Bueckers and Geno Auriemma didn't speak for two weeks during UConn's 2025 championship run - CBS Sports
description: From the early days of Geno Auriemma's attempts to put UConn on the map to how much a hug from Auriemma meant to Paige Bueckers after wi
body:
From the early days of Geno Auriemma's attempts to put UConn on the map to how much a hug from Auriemma meant to Paige Bueckers after winning a national championship, the new Apple TV documentary "The Dynasty: UConn Huskies" shares insight on the most successful program in college basketball history.Since taking over in 1985, Auriemma has led UConn to 12 national titles. His methods for getting the most out of his players might be controversial, but the results speak for themselves. This three-part series shares more about his relationship with former stars and what it really takes to become a dynasty.Clips of Bueckers and teammate Azzi Fudd confirming their romantic relationship in the documentary went viral earlier this week, but there is a lot more worth discussing. Here are some of the major takeaways:Auriemma and Bueckers didn't speak for weeksThe emotional hug between Auriemma and Bueckers toward the end of the 2025 national championship game only lasted a few seconds, but it meant more than we could have imagined.
"That was just everything that we had been through up until that point, just the emotions of it and just everything coming together," Bueckers said. "The times where we hated each other, where we loved each other. Everything that me and coach had been through to that point, it was just embodied in that hug."
After Bueckers' historic freshman season, she faced one of her toughest mental challenges ever when she tore her ACL in 2022. She was having panic attacks at night and couldn't help but wonder, "What if I never come back the same?" Things did not get much easier once she got back on the court.Auriemma wanted Bueckers to be a more assertive leader and pushed her especially hard during the 2024-25 season, her last year at UConn. This created a lot of tension between them and at one point they didn't talk to each other for weeks. Bueckers said she was "just showing up to practice and existing."
"She had said to me, 'I came back for my fifth year because I thought we're gonna have things figured out and it was going to be fun,'" Fudd said. "She basically said it's the exact opposite of that."Auriemma said the need for stronger leadership showed up even more in a game against Tennessee. The players themselves knew something had to change as even then-sophomore KK Arnold said, "Everybody's head was everywhere, kind of like not knowing where to go." The Lady Vols had not beaten UConn since 2007, but their drought was over when they bested the Huskies on Feb. 6, 2025."That was the hardest loss, I think, in quite some time," Auriemma said. "Bottom line is, Paige needed to change.... So I took a risk and I said, 'She is either gonna quit or she's gonna change.' So I tried to hurt her like losing hurts."
The next film session, Auriemma was tougher on Bueckers than ever before and questioned why her teammates should follow her. She said it was tough to understand it at first, but when it finally clicked, she called a players-only meeting to let her teammates know she was going to be more assertive and start holding everyone accountable. The turning point of the season happened later that month when the Huskies blew out South Carolina 87-58 and snapped the Gamecocks' 71-home game winning streak. UConn didn't lose a single game after that and eventually beat South Carolina again in the NCAA Tournament championship game. Bueckers was able to walk away as a national champion with a whole different outlook on life."Coach has a very unique way of getting the best out of his players," she said. "And at times it was difficult being able to handle that burden, but to be in that moment, it all paid off on the biggest stage. I think that just completely changed my life."
If you want to go down memory lane, here is a recap of Bueckers last college basketball game.
        
            
                'It's destiny': UConn's Paige Bueckers finally wins national championship to cap off decorated college career
                
                    Isabel Gonzalez                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
'It's all worth it'Even Rebecca Lobo -- the foundational superstar who helped put the program on the national map -- had some difficult moments with Auriemma. As associate head coach Chris Dailey pointed out, the staff was always the toughest on their best player in order to help them reach their full potential."He was incredibly hard on me," Lobo said. "'You are the worst post player in America. The dumbest smart person in America.' Like, yelling at me constantly, which was really hard for me as a 17- and 18-year old to understand because no one had really ever coached me in that way."
As the program continued to grow, players had to deal with the tough coaching and the incredibly high expectations that come with being the team to beat. Current Vanderbilt coach Shea Ralph won a championship at UConn as a player in 2000, and later spent 13 seasons as one of Auriemma's assistant coaches. She said that for players at UConn there is a "heaviness" that exists because the expectations are so high at such an elite program. However, she said she didn't regret going through it because the experience made her better.When it's all said and done, success came at a price that UConn greats were happy to pay -- including Diana Taurasi, who won three national championships with the Huskies."I think in all these stories, through the championships and all the different classes, all the workouts, all the practices, all the moments we have to look in the mirror and face all the things that you hate about yourself, there is just this moment of like, 'It is worth it,'" Taurasi said. "It actually is worth it. All of it is worth it. All of it.'"
Auriemma's biggest rival: Pat SummittBefore UConn became UConn, Tennessee was the team to beat under the leadership of Pat Summitt. The relationship between Auriemma and Summitt started out pleasant, but tensions grew when UConn started gaining more success.A lot of it had to do with the competitive nature of the sport, but also the difference in their personalities. Although both coached their teams hard, Summitt held a more formal and decorous public image while Auriemma was blunt and outspoken.They used to play often, but their feud led to Summitt ending their regular-season series in the summer of 2007. It was a complicated relationship, but despite their differences, there was a lot of respect between them.
When Summitt passed away in 2016 due to Alzheimer's disease, Auriemma said the loss hit him hard."When this happened with Pat, it's a contemporary of yours and it really hits home," he said. "We were different people. Grew up different, maybe viewed the world differently. But at the same time, as competitors we were the same in a lot of ways."Washington Post columnist Sally Jenkins, a close friend of Summitt, also shared an insight into their relationship.
"I think there is a buried love between great competitors," she said. "Pat and Geno, they couldn't see it for themselves necessarily, but I know for a fact that's what Pat felt at the end: love for Geno."
Retirement?Auriemma has already accomplished it all, and then some. He is the winningest coach in NCAA Division I basketball history with 1,288 career wins, and counting. His 12 national championships with the same program are also a record that seems almost impossible to break.His family moved from Italy to the United States when he was seven years old and he said that wanting to belong in this country was part of why he wanted to succeed so badly. But at this point in his career, he has nothing left to prove.
After the 2025 national championship, Dailey asked Auriemma if he was retiring. "F--- yeah, I'm retiring," he told her. "We should."Somewhere along the way he changed his mind and decided to stick around. However, he joked about how if he were smart, he would have said it into the microphone."The question is, what makes it the end?" he said. "When does the actual story end? You never know."

And there are just three teams that hit that threshold in two of the three groups: Air Force, Georgia and Notre Dame.
The Fighting Irish could have one of the best defensive units in the country this season, returning eight starters on that side. And the continuity is spread out, too, with 80% of secondary snaps, 76% of linebacker snaps and 60% of defensive line snaps returning. BYU is the only other program in the FBS that hits the 60% mark across all three position groups.Georgia, meanwhile, brings back the highest percentage of snaps among the FBS' front-seven units. That's particularly notable after the Bulldogs posted a 4.2% sack rate in 2025, their lowest under Kirby Smart and the seventh-worst mark among Power Four teams. With more continuity up front, Georgia has a chance to turn that weakness into a strength in 2026.Air Force leads the FBS in percentage of returning defensive snaps, with its linebacker corps and secondary ranking No. 1 nationally, but the Falcons retained just 24% of their snaps along the defensive line.
At the bottom end, the turnover is stark. Each of the 10 teams with the lowest percentage of returning defensive snaps brings back fewer than 20% across all three position groups. Washington State is the only team in the FBS below 10% in all three, a reflection of the massive overhaul on that side of the ball. More than 20 defensive players transferred out of the program, including a dozen who followed former coach Jimmy Rogers to Iowa State.Why returning snaps still matters for roster buildingReturning snaps aren't a perfect predictor of success, and they're not meant to be treated as one. Teams can and do rebuild quickly; Indiana is the obvious recent reminder that a major overhaul can still turn into immediate success.But those situations are the exception, not the rule.More often, returning snaps help explain why some teams might start faster than others. They don't guarantee wins, but they do point to stability: fewer unknowns in execution, more familiarity on both sides of the ball and a roster that has already logged meaningful game reps together. That kind of continuity tends to shorten the adjustment period in August and September.
Think of it less as a prediction tool and more as a baseline. It doesn't tell you who will break out, but it does help explain who has the cleanest runway to do so. In a sport defined by roster churn, that starting point still matters.

        Anthony Hernandez and Gregory Rodrigues fight very differently, but share a common theme: decisions are not part of the design. Hernandez breaks spirits while Rodrigues breaks faces. Their philosophies collide at UFC Fight Night in Sacramento, California.Hernandez (15-3, 1 NC) is in a bad mood. His normally relaxed demeanor has been replaced with a serious edge. He's not feeling particularly social heading into Saturday's main event. Hernandez breaks opponents with relentless pace and pressure -- his appetite to apply that on Fight Night borders on disturbing. "I want to hurt somebody, man. I want to finish somebody," Hernandez  told CBS Sports HQ. "I want to make somebody hate their f---ing life."  Hernandez is one fight removed from a non-title loss to reigning middleweight champion Sean Strickland. The fight would've launched "Fluffy" into the title scene. Instead, Strickland knocked him out and went on to reclaim the title. He took the loss honorably, going on to train with Strickland and his camp.

They were nothing but respectful."
You wouldn't know that Rodrigues (19-6) is a decorated jiu-jitsu athlete by his mixed martial arts career. He hasn't achieved a submission win in nearly a decade. It's not that he can't; it's that he doesn't need to. Rodrigues is blessed with ferocious knockout power. Appropriately nicknamed "Robocop," Rodrigues marches forward and short-circuits his opponents. On a 6-1 run with surging momentum, it feels like now or never for Rodrigues to break into the middleweight top 10.
"There are two things a coach can't put in a fighter: a heavy hand and heart. I'm born with both," Rodrigues told CBS Sports' Brian Campbell. "I'm not looking for the knockout; it just happens. I'm a well-rounded guy. I'm ready for 25 minutes. I want to be inside the Octagon the whole fight. Whatever happens before [the final bell], that's a bonus."Elsewhere on Saturday, heavyweights collide in the co-main event when Vitor Petrino takes on Serghei Spivac. Petrino enters on a three-fight win streak after moving up to heavyweight. Spivac, meanwhile, bounced back from a pair of defeats with a win in February. Plus, former middleweights now meet at light heavyweight when Reinier de Ridder takes on Roman Dolidze. And fresh off a contract winning performance on Contender Series, heavyweight Anthony Wint makes his UFC debut against Terrance Chatman.
